Welcome. This guide is written for **new TAs / graders / discussion-section leaders** for a course taught from *Statistical Inference via Data Science: A ModernDive into R and the Tidyverse*. Read it once before the term starts (~30 minutes), then keep it open as a reference.

::: {.callout-tip title="Coordinate with your instructor"}
Every course is different. This packet describes ModernDive-typical patterns; your specific instructor's emphasis, grading scale, and discussion-section format may differ. The first time you read something here that contradicts what your instructor said: **ask the instructor**. Their version wins.
:::

---

# Section 1 — The TA role

What you ARE responsible for (typically):

- Running 1-2 discussion sections per week (50-75 min each)
- Holding 2-4 office hours per week
- Grading 1-2 problem sets per week
- Answering Piazza / Slack / forum questions
- Coming to weekly TA meetings with the instructor

What you are NOT responsible for (and should refer up):

- Re-teaching lecture content if students missed class (point them to the textbook + slides)
- Diagnosing serious mental-health concerns (refer to campus resources)
- Negotiating grades after they're posted (route to instructor)
- Adjusting course policy (deadlines, late work, etc.) for individuals (route to instructor)
- Answering questions about whether a student should drop the course (route to advisor)

---

# Section 2 — Five things that will save you time

**1. The misconceptions cheat-sheet.** Before any office-hour shift, skim [misconceptions.html](misconceptions.html) for the chapter you're covering. Most "I don't understand" questions map to a distractor option you can name. ("Ah, you're thinking X — that's a common reading. Here's why it's actually Y.")

**2. The solutions site.** [solutions/index.html](solutions/index.html) has worked solutions to every end-of-chapter exercise. Search by exercise number, NOT by re-deriving from scratch. (Tip: don't show students the solution before they've struggled. Show structure first.)

**3. The Quick checks.** Every chapter has them at the end. They're the assigned-reading concept checks. If a student asks "what's important from this chapter", point to Quick checks first.

**4. The facilitator notes.** [facilitator-notes/index.html](facilitator-notes/index.html) gives a lecture-plan-style view of each chapter. Great for prepping a discussion section script.

**5. The active-learning prompts.** [active-learning.html](active-learning.html) has ready-to-use non-MCQ discussion prompts per chapter. Pick 1-2 per section.

---

# Section 3 — How to run a discussion section

Standard 50-minute format that works for most ModernDive sections:

| Time | Activity | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| 0:00 - 0:05 | **Warm-up** — 1 prediction prompt or Quick-check question | Settle in; surface what they remember |
| 0:05 - 0:15 | **Confusion sweep** — "What from this week was hard?" | You teach to actual gaps, not assumed ones |
| 0:15 - 0:35 | **Worked example** — walk a hard exercise as a class | Show YOUR thinking, not just the answer |
| 0:35 - 0:45 | **Pair work** — students try a similar problem; you circulate | Active engagement; you spot misunderstandings |
| 0:45 - 0:50 | **Wrap** — preview next week; remind of office hours / deadlines | Closure |

Variants:

- **All-coding sections** (lab-style): replace 0:15-0:35 with live coding; 0:35-0:45 with student-paired exercises
- **Hybrid lecture/discussion**: replace 0:00-0:05 with a 5-min MCQ poll using slide variants
- **Online sections**: 0:15-0:35 in main room, 0:35-0:45 in breakout pairs

Don't lecture for more than 10 minutes straight. After 10 minutes of monologue, students stop listening; they need a chance to talk or think.

---

# Section 4 — How to answer "I'm stuck"

This is the most common request. A bad answer ("here's the code") teaches helplessness. A good answer ("show me where you are; what have you tried?") teaches debugging.

**The diagnostic ladder** — work UP it, not down:

1. **"Show me your code and the error message."** No advice without seeing the actual thing. (50% of questions resolve here: the student misread their own code.)
2. **"What did you expect to happen?"** Surfaces the mental model. Often the model is wrong, not the code.
3. **"What have you tried so far?"** If they haven't tried anything, hand them back a SMALL next step. ("Try `glimpse(your_df)` first and tell me what you see.")
4. **"Let's break this into pieces."** Many "I'm stuck" problems are 2-3 nested steps. Untangle them one at a time.
5. **"Have you Googled the error message verbatim?"** Modeling adult debugging behavior is a course outcome.
6. **As a LAST resort: pair-debug it together.** Type with them, not for them.

What NOT to say:

- ❌ "Here's the code." (Teaches dependence.)
- ❌ "It's in the textbook on page X." (Dismissive; they already missed it.)
- ❌ "That should be obvious." (Never. Never. Never.)

What TO say:

- ✓ "Let's look at your error message together — what's the first word?"
- ✓ "What does the function `filter()` expect as its first argument?"
- ✓ "I see what you tried. The next thing I'd check is..."

---

# Section 5 — How to grade

**Read the rubric first.** Always. Even if you've graded the same assignment in past terms; rubrics evolve.

**Grade horizontally, not vertically.** Grade Question 1 across ALL students, then Question 2 across ALL students. Calibrates fairness; faster.

**Calibration session before grading.** With other TAs + instructor: pick 2-3 anonymized examples (one strong, one weak, one mediocre). Grade together. Resolve disagreements. THEN grade alone.

**Comment policy** — give every student exactly:

- ONE thing they did well (specific, not "good job!")
- ONE thing to work on (actionable)

That's it. More comments aren't more learning; they're more for the grader to manage.

**Suspected academic dishonesty.** If you see two submissions with identical idiosyncratic code: flag it for the instructor; don't accuse the student yourself. Document with screenshots; let the instructor handle the conversation.

**Late work.** Follow the syllabus exactly. If the syllabus says "10% off per day", that's 10% off per day. Don't make exceptions; route requests to the instructor.

See the [rubrics library](rubrics.html) for the canonical analytic rubrics.

---

# Section 6 — Office hours

**Start on time, end on time.** TAs who run over teach students that "office hours" means "when the TA is in the room until they leave."

**Group similar questions.** If three students walk in with versions of the same question, work it out on the whiteboard for all of them. Saves repetition; builds peer learning.

**Have students articulate the question first.** Even if obvious: "Tell me what you're trying to do, in your own words, before showing me the code." 30% of office-hour questions resolve here.

**Don't let one student monopolize.** If a student has been there 20+ minutes and others are waiting, say: "Let me get to a couple more questions and come back to you." Be matter-of-fact, not apologetic.

**Trickier questions:** if you don't know, say "I don't know, let me check with the instructor and get back to you on Piazza." NEVER make something up. Students remember.

# Section 7 — Per-chapter notes

For each chapter, this section gives you: what to emphasize, what trips students, and 3 worked examples you can pull into a section.

## Chapter 1 — Getting started

**Emphasize**: R vs RStudio distinction. Installation. The pattern: `install.packages(...)` (one time) + `library(...)` (every session). Tab completion in RStudio.

**Trips students**:

- Confusing R and RStudio ("I downloaded R but where's the program with all the panels?")
- "Why do I have to type `library()` every time?"
- Case sensitivity (`Glimpse()` vs `glimpse()`)
- Forgetting to assign with `<-` (or `=`)
- Mac users: command-key vs control-key confusion

**Section game plan**: spend 70% of the time getting EVERY student to run a `library(dplyr); glimpse(starwars)` chunk. The students who don't get this working in week 1 fall behind for the term.

## Chapter 2 — Data visualization

**Emphasize**: aesthetics MAP variables; settings are constants. `geom_xxx()` is the visual mark. ggplot is **additive** (`+` not `|>`).

**Trips students**:

- The `aes()` boundary: `aes(color = species)` (color depends on data) vs `color = "blue"` (constant).
- Forgetting `+` between layers.
- "Why does my plot have no data?" (forgot `geom_xxx()` after `ggplot()`).
- Default themes look ugly; students think THEIR plot is ugly. Teach `theme_minimal()` early.

**Section game plan**: live-code a single plot end-to-end with student-suggested variables. Iterate the title, axis labels, color, theme. Show that "polish" is just N more lines.

## Chapter 3 — Data wrangling

**Emphasize**: each `dplyr` verb returns a data frame; you can chain. The pipe `|>` reads left-to-right like English. `group_by()` + `summarize()` is the workhorse pattern.

**Trips students**:

- Confusing `select()` (columns) and `filter()` (rows).
- Single `=` vs double `==` in `filter()`.
- "Where does `n()` come from?" (it's a `dplyr` verb only valid inside `summarize()` / `mutate()`).
- Forgetting `group_by()` doesn't visibly change anything until `summarize()` runs.
- Joins: which columns get matched? Why does `full_join` return more rows than I expected?

**Section game plan**: pose a question ("which carrier had the worst on-time record in 2013?"), then BUILD the pipe with students one verb at a time. Show what each intermediate step returns.

## Chapter 4 — Data importing and tidy data

**Emphasize**: tidy data = each variable a column, each observation a row, each value a cell. `read_csv()` from `readr`. `pivot_longer()` / `pivot_wider()` reshape.

**Trips students**:

- "Long" vs "wide" intuition takes a couple examples to settle.
- Reading data from URLs vs local files.
- Encoding issues (utf-8 vs latin1) for international data.
- Date parsing (`readr` often gets it right, but not always).

**Section game plan**: bring an untidy dataset (or have students bring one from their lives). Tidy it together. Discuss why each move makes downstream analysis easier.

## Chapter 5 — Basic regression

**Emphasize**: intercept (predicted $y$ when $x = 0$), slope (predicted change in $y$ per unit change in $x$), residual (observed - fitted). Categorical predictors get reference-coded.

**Trips students**:

- Interpreting the slope WITH UNITS ("4.2 mpg per 1000 lbs decrease", not "4.2").
- "What's that one extra coefficient when species is categorical?" → reference coding.
- $R^2$ misinterpretation (see ethics scenarios + four-corners in [active learning](active-learning.html)).

**Section game plan**: fit `lm(mpg ~ wt)` on `mtcars`. Walk through every number in the output. Then add a categorical predictor and re-walk.

## Chapter 6 — Multiple regression

**Emphasize**: "controlling for" / "holding constant" interpretation. Interaction = slope depends on another variable. Reading `summary()` outputs.

**Trips students**:

- Why does adding a predictor CHANGE the slope on the first one? → Confounding / partial associations.
- Interactions: `*` vs `+` in the formula syntax.
- Predicting with `predict()` — what shape does `newdata` need to be?
- Categorical × continuous interactions visualized.

**Section game plan**: use the housing example (or penguins). First fit `price ~ size`. Then `price ~ size + condition`. Then `price ~ size * condition`. Watch the slope move. Demand domain interpretation at each step.

## Chapter 7 — Sampling

**Emphasize**: sampling distribution (statistic across MANY samples) is NOT the data distribution (one sample). Standard error = SD of the sampling distribution. Larger $n$ → narrower sampling distribution.

**Trips students**:

- Population vs sample vs sampling distribution — three different things, all related.
- "Why does the standard error shrink with $n$ but not the standard deviation?"
- The bowl-of-balls virtual experiment confuses students initially; persist with it.

**Section game plan**: redo the `pennies_sample` simulation with `n = 25, 50, 100, 200`. Plot the sampling distributions side by side. Build intuition visually.

## Chapter 8 — Confidence intervals

**Emphasize**: a CI is a range of plausible values for an UNKNOWN PARAMETER. The 95% refers to the procedure ("if I repeated this, 95% of intervals would catch the parameter"), not to "the probability the parameter is in this one interval."

**Trips students**:

- The "probability the parameter is in the interval" wording (it's wrong! the parameter is fixed; the interval is random).
- Bootstrap: "why is resampling from your sample valid?" (because your sample is your best estimate of the population).
- Width of CI: what makes it narrow vs wide? ($n$, confidence level, $\\sigma$).

**Section game plan**: see the [four-corners prompt](active-learning.html#chapter-8--confidence-intervals) on CI interpretations. Run that as a section. Spend 20+ minutes on this — it's THE major-misunderstanding chapter.

## Chapter 9 — Hypothesis testing

**Emphasize**: $H_0$ vs $H_a$ are claims about a parameter. $p$-value = probability of getting data this extreme OR MORE, ASSUMING $H_0$ is true. Failing to reject $\\ne$ accepting.

**Trips students**:

- The conditional in the $p$-value definition. Always.
- "If $p > 0.05$, is $H_0$ true?" (No. We just didn't find enough evidence against it.)
- "Significant" in statistics ($p < \\alpha$) vs everyday ("important"). Two different things.
- Type I vs Type II error (one-line drill: "Type I = false alarm; Type II = miss").

**Section game plan**: see the [four-corners prompt](active-learning.html#chapter-9--hypothesis-testing) on what a $p$-value means. Walk through the `infer` pipeline step-by-step on the gender-discrimination case.

## Chapter 10 — Inference for regression

**Emphasize**: slope is a STATISTIC (varies sample to sample); its sampling distribution has a standard error. LINE conditions for theory-based inference. Bootstrap if LINE breaks.

**Trips students**:

- Going from "the slope is 4.2" (Ch 5) to "the slope has a sampling distribution centered at 4.2 with SE 0.8" (Ch 10) — same model, different mental model.
- LINE: which condition each diagnostic plot addresses.
- Reading CI for slope vs CI for prediction (different widths!).

**Section game plan**: refit a Ch 5 model. Then run `infer`'s bootstrap workflow. Compare bootstrap CI to theory-based CI. Discuss when they agree / disagree.

## Chapter 11 — Tell your story

**Emphasize**: data analysis is communication. Effective communication = understanding your audience + ruthless prioritization + honest about uncertainty.

**Trips students**:

- "What's the headline?" — students often bury the lede.
- Tables vs charts: when to use which.
- Citation of data sources.
- Writing for a non-technical audience.

**Section game plan**: do a peer-critique session. Bring 1-2 anonymized capstone reports from past terms (with permission). Have students mark them up. Compare critiques. Most students learn more from critiquing than from writing.

---

# Section 8 — Weekly TA-meeting checklist

Bring to your weekly meeting with the instructor:

- This week's confusion-sweep results (what students said was hard)
- Common errors you saw in office hours
- Any flagged academic-integrity concerns
- Any student in serious distress (academic OR personal)
- Grading consistency questions
- Anything in next week's content you're not 100% sure about

---

# Section 9 — Self-care

You will burn out if you don't manage your time. Some rules of thumb:

- Hard-cap office hours. If you said 2-4pm, leave at 4. The line outside the door at 4:01pm is not your problem; it's the instructor's signal to schedule more hours.
- Hard-cap forum response time. Pick "I respond by 9pm M-F". Stick to it. The 11pm Sunday panic-question can wait until Monday.
- One day a week off. Genuinely off. Phone notifications off for course channels.
- Talk to your TA peers. The hardest students, the impossible-feeling weeks — every TA has them. You're not alone.
- If you're drowning, tell the instructor early. Adjustments are possible. Silence isn't.

::: {.callout-note title="One more thing"}
You're not in this role to be liked. You're here to help students learn. Those two are mostly aligned, but when they conflict — when a student wants a hint and learning would be better served by struggle — choose learning. Students remember the TAs who pushed them.
:::
